extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and students interested in press freedom and Maldivian politics
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of censorship and press-freedom issues in the Maldives, reporting international index scores, notable incidents (blog shutdowns, arrests, website blocking), and referencing domestic media regulation. Useful as a country-level overview of censorship practices and indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: International press freedom indexes / overall ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Maldives 'ranks from the middle to the top third of international indexes of press freedom', indicating a large degree of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Freedom House (2011) — Maldives scored 50, labeled 'partly free'; Reporters Without Borders (2024) — ranked Maldives 106th of 180. These indexes are used as comparative metrics to evaluate the country's overall press freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom House Freedom of the Press score
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 2011 Freedom House Freedom of the Press annual report, the Maldives scores a 50, or 'partly free'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This numeric score and qualitative label (e.g., 'partly free') serve as an evaluative criterion for assessing press freedom over time and relative to other countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters Without Borders (RSF) press freedom ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters Without Borders ranked the Maldives as having the 106th freest press in the world (of 180 ranked nations) in 2024.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RSF rankings provide an international comparative indicator used to judge the state of media freedom in the Maldives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-based grounds for censorship (religion-related restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Communications Authority of the Maldives (CAM) shut down the blog of journalist Ismail Khilath Rasheed on the order of the Ministry of Islamic Affairs on the grounds that the site contained 'anti-Islamic material'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates a substantive legal/policy standard applied in practice: content deemed 'anti-Islamic' may be grounds for blocking or removal. The article uses this incident as an example of religious restrictions shaping censorship practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: State action: blocking/unblocking of news websites
rubrics_metrics.description: On 22 December 2023, CAM blocked two anti-government news websites; they were unblocked four days later after condemnation by rights groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government blocking (temporary or permanent) of news sites is presented as an observable metric/manifestation of censorship; timing and reversals (blocking then unblocking) are relevant to assessing practice and responsiveness to pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest/detention of journalists and campaigners
rubrics_metrics.description: Ismail Khilath Rasheed was arrested following attacks and pressure by political/religious actors; human-rights groups protested and he was released following advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrests, unclear charges, and detention of journalists or activists are cited as indicators of repression and limitations on freedom of expression; reactions from groups like Amnesty International and UN bodies are used as context for evaluating such incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic legal framework: Maldives Media and Broadcasting Regulation Law
rubrics_metrics.description: The article references the 'Maldives Media and Broadcasting Regulation Law' as relevant to media regulation and censorship in the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory/regulatory instruments (laws governing media and broadcasting) are structural criteria that determine permissible content and administrative powers (e.g., to shut down sites or revoke licenses); they form the legal basis against which incidents are assessed.
